item.description:
Elsewhere on the site, you can read a big reveal piece that outlines the new game from former Disco Elysium devs under the name of Summer Eternal - an "incendiary RPG" fusing the best bits of text-heavy isometric role-playing games with the world-building and player agency of an immersive sim. It's bold, it's ambitious, and it's still in development, and if it all comes off, it could be something really special.
But here's the most intriguing part, as far as I'm concerned: the developers are giving you the chance to have a say over how the company is run. If you buy anything from the studio - including the 500 page Anthology that was formally announced today - you are welcome to join the Players Non-Profit community organisation, which owns 5 percent of Summer Eternal and takes part in the studio's governance.
"The Players Non-Profit owns a five percent share in our studio. The other 95 percent is divided between other stakeholders: full-time workers, freelancers and investors in Summer Eternal," explains the studio in a press release. But what exactly does that mean? Well, it's a long and complicated explanation - as these things often are - but the central point is this: every player is a member of the board.
In a late stage capitalist world, that might seem a little… well, radical. But Summer Eternal holds community and developer ownership as one of its core philosophical tenets. This is more a collective than it is a company. "Although five percent is a shy amount, it's still powerful enough for the player-pool to summon a general Assembly to discuss a topic," says Summer Eternal. "This non-profit will be the 'voice of the gamers' in an experimental attempt to formalise the community decision-making in game development. The non-profit can use the game revenue to organise events, support union-work, or whatever their assembly (comprised of all members) decides on."
The primary function of this collective, per Summer Eternal itself, is to "provide transparency and actionable means of interception to those who've put their trust in us". Ergo: don't like a feature in the game? You can challenge the devs. Don't want a specific mechanic, or character, or scene? You have a right to make your voice heard. It's not something we often see in games - studios commonly work 'behind closed doors' until they've got a nearly shippable build to show, and then we might get a demo or the press may see a build before general release. There are, of course, some studios that buck that trend with Early Access initiatives, but they are hit and miss for studios. This more communal approach to development is far more rare, and - in my eyes, at least - exciting.
I have read a fair amount about Summer Eternal's structure and its vision for community-facing development through its Anthology; part-treatise about Summer Eternals radical development ideas and the politics of making games in 2026, part-development diary about Red Rooster. It includes interviews about the state of games and tech with economists Yanis Varoufakis and Richard Wolff, a chat with science fiction visionary (and one of my favourite authors) Ted Chiang, conversations with Bioware veterans Mark Darrah and David Gaider, as well as stories from worker-run organizations such as the UVW-CWA, Aftermath, and Peregrine Coast Press.
If you'd like a copy yourself, you can purchase one here - it's €69 for the Standard edition, and €99 for the Deluxe Firestarter bundle that comes with a vinyl and additional merch. And, naturally, if you buy a copy of the book, you will also be entitled to a membership in the Summer Eternal Players Non-Profit organisation. You can join that initiative here.

item.title: Cyberleek, the leaker who's been releasing footage from Grand Theft Auto 6 for weeks now, is seemingly done posting leaks. Cyberleek released a new - seemingly final - video today which supposedly shows parts of the game's ending. Read more
item.description:
Cyberleek, the leaker who's been releasing footage from Grand Theft Auto 6 for weeks now, is seemingly done posting leaks. Cyberleek released a new - seemingly final - video today which supposedly shows parts of the game's ending.
The leaker has indicated they may be done sharing footage as their goal of pumping their crypto coin had failed. Cyberleek recently said they'd release a 200GB build of the game if the coin hits $30m market cap, which it's nowhere near doing.
The coin has crashed in recent weeks after a major bump that coincided with the release of leaked footage showing co-protagonist Lucia fully naked, shortly after they released footage of co-protagonist Jason also nude.
Eurogamer has seen the latest footage, and it's not as dramatic as Cyberleek initially made it out to be. The footage does not appear to be of the game's ending sequence or final cutscene, though the location of where the action takes place could be a spoiler. The four-minute video ends with a montage of various locations and flyover footage of a city, set to Journey's Don't Stop Believin'.
There may be something there, but when viewed without proper context, it's hard to say what's actually being spoiled. Still, the footage is best avoided if you want to jump into the game fresh.
At the time of writing, Cyberleek's memecoin's market cap has dropped to $1.2m just three days after reaching its peak of $7.8m. It also seems they've abandoned the initial plan to tie certain gameplay leaks to the coin's market cap.
"The leeks stop here. For now," Cyberleek allegedly wrote, though it's worth keeping in mind that the leaker reappeared last week after going to ground following their initial leaks in August, seemingly in response to Rockstar parent company Take-Two initiating a massive investigation and issuing subpoenas to Discord and Microsoft.
Given recent history, Cyberleek could simply re-emerge yet again with a new scam and more footage. GTA 6's 19th November official launch is not far off, however, so their window is closing.

item.description:
Back in 2024, we heard about the formation of Summer Eternal: a new studio composed of Disco Elysium writer and world-builder, Argo Tuulik, and other veteran ZA/UM staff such as Dora Klindžić, Anastasia Ivanova, and Michael Oswell. Aleksandar Gavrilović, secretary of the Croatian Game Development Alliance, and Lenval Brown, Disco Elysium's narrator, are also part of the crew.
Since then, we've heard nothing from the new collective, but earlier this month, the studio got in contact with me to gauge interest in the Summer Eternal Anthology, a 500-page physical book that's part-treatise on the cultural and labour impact of the video game industry, and part-development journal for its newly-announced "incendiary RPG", Red Rooster.
In Red Rooster, you play as Redrick Roost, a white-collar inmate thrust into the role of an arson investigator who partners up with an opiate-dependent mathematician. Together, they investigate a string of arson that all seems to connect to Redrick's brother who is none other than - you guessed it! - the city's fire chief. Per Summer Eternal, the game is set in a "fractalised border archipelago" of the tri-partie city of Arta-Tantor. It's all very political alternate history stuff, with a "strong science-fiction undercurrent". As Red Rooster's tagline puts it, "Fight fires to get to the truth of your world. Start fires to get to the truth about yourself."
Summer Eternal is calling Red Rooster an "incendiary, physics-driven RPG combining the best of cerebral, worldbuilding-rich RPGs with the genetics of physics-driven immersive sims". Very ambitious, then. The studio also notes the game is "fully physics-driven" and full of objects you can move, manipulate, and burn - the team wants you to "exert your physical existence" upon the world. "RPG worlds are often static, frozen maps," it says. "We're aiming to build the urban archipelago of Arta-Tantor into a reactive playground of physical interactivity and evolving human stories through scripted and emergent events."
Red Rooster is being built in Unreal Engine to make use of advanced physics engine features, and the studio adds it's "breaking away from isometric constraints to drop you into a three-dimensional world with dynamic camera movement. " Elsewhere in the release, it name-drops Expedition 33's Sandfall Interactive, noting the collective is aiming for a "double-A production budget" similar to the "compact team" that worked on 2025's breakout RPG.
Summer Eternal says the game is "nearing the end of pre-production" and that an internal playable tech demo already exists. The book shows a little of this, and while I appreciate the team is trying to put distance between itself and Disco Elysium, you can't help notice the similarities in some aspects. Below, you can see a quick pic I snapped of the eponymous Red Rooster - he bears more than a passing resemblance to Harrier 'Harry' Du Bois, right?
Elsewhere in the game, there's 'The Coop', which is reminiscent of Disco Elysium's psychological manifestations in the 'Thought Cabinet'. Here, Red's internal mental space is populated by roosters; versions of himself that represent different motivations, urges, and personalities. Summer Eternal references games like Exanima, Half-Life: Alyx, Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura, Planescape: Torment, and Larian's Divinity engine games as inspiration. Influences outside of games include Chris Carter's Millenium, Fringe, Netflix's Dark, Better Call Saul, Fargo, and the works of Ted Chiang and John Steinbeck.
A lot of this information comes from the book that's been used to announce the game, and the Summer Eternal Anthology is a very interesting read. It includes interviews about the state of games and tech with economists Yanis Varoufakis and Richard Wolff, a chat with science fiction visionary (and one of my favourite authors) Ted Chiang, conversations with Bioware veterans Mark Darrah and David Gaider, as well as stories from worker-run organizations such as the UVW-CWA, Aftermath, and Peregrine Coast Press (who are wonderfully described as "paper perverts"). If you'd like a copy yourself, you can purchase one here - it's €69 for the Standard edition, and €99 for the Deluxe Firestarter bundle that comes with a vinyl and additional merch.
If you buy a copy of the book, you will also be entitled to a membership in the Summer Eternal Players Non-Profit organisation, which owns five percent of Summer Eternal; giving you a vote on matters regarding studio governance, and having a say in how five percent of profits generated by Red Rooster are used in the future. You can join that initiative here.
Summer Eternal, of course, isn't the only studio to have been born from the fracturing of ZA/UM's original team. There's also Longdue, an independent studio comprising former Disco Elysium staff, and Dark Math Games, a team that refers to itself as a "breakaway group from the original development team of Disco Elysium". ZA/UM also carried on as a development unit, and the studio launched Zero Parades: For Dead Spies back in June, before laying off a large chunk of its remaining staff. Prior to the multi-part split of Disco Elysium talent, game director Robert Kurvitz and art director Aleksander Rostov alleged that ZA/UM management had gained ownership of the studio and its intellectual property fraudulently, with the two claiming that they were "summarily fired and cut off from our life's work" after they began asking for financial records from ZA/UM's new owners. Counter-allegations of mismanagement and misconduct followed, and it only got messier from there.
Back in 2024, in a feature I worked on at VG247, game director Argo Tuulick told the site "he'd rather under-promise and over-deliver" when it comes to this game. This book, though, seems to have moved on from that maxim, and may well be one of the most ambitious project statements I've ever seen. It's made me incredibly excited, too; to see a studio commit to a worker- and player-funded model, using a game this ambitious as its banner, is something that can instil just a little bit of hope in an industry fighting to stay afloat under the yoke of late-stage capitalism.

item.description:
I honestly can't tell you how many times I've completed The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, let alone how many hours I've spent in its bucolic version of Hyrule. Though, when I told my Mum about the upcoming remake she said, 'Oh the one with the music,' in a tone I've decided to interpret as delight. I think that says a lot about how much of a fixture this game was in my life, in our household.
The existence of the Switch 2 remake isn't a surprise - it's a very safe bet for Nintendo - and it's not the first time Ocarina has been remade either. (And I highly doubt the last.) Yet, it is the first time the game feels like it's been reworked from the ground up. A proposition that left me wondering if this version can live up to the game that originally turned me into a Zelda fanatic.
Let's start with the most obvious change - the graphics. The art style got a real mixed reaction after the first full trailer dropped. A proper marmite situation. You either love the peculiar 'haunted doll' art style, or you think Link and Zelda are born from the darkest depths of the uncanny valley. I fell into the 'love' category upon my first viewing but, the more I rewatched the trailer, the more I started to worry it was all a little too much. Having now played parts of the remake, I'm happy to say my gut instinct was, indeed, correct.
Unlike the 3DS remake, which glossed and smoothed the rough edges of the original N64 graphics, Ocarina on the Switch 2 rewrites them completely. In doing so, new life has been breathed into Hyrule, giving it texture and depth. You can find it in the little things; the rough tree bark, the setting sun slowly inking the sky orange, the contrast between the vibrant Hyrule Castle Town and the nature born Kokiri Forest. Best of all, the character designs don't feel out of place at all. Instead, they look completely at home in the landscape. I would adore a remake of Majora's Mask in this art style - what a joy it would be to see it so wonderfully twisted and surreal and unsettling. Imagine the moon! In Ocarina though, together the repainted world and characters capture the essence of what the game has always been - a fairy tale. A story of good intentions gone awry and a brave soul whose determination and a very sharp sword save the land.
But there are some things that take some getting used to. The jumping! Now, I'm not a fan of jumping in either real life or games, so the removal of auto-jumping was a change I'll admit to being a little miffed about. Yet, I can see the logic behind the decision. It eases the gap somewhat for players whose introduction to the Zelda series was Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom by bringing the Ocarina control scheme more inline with those games. You can even change the jump button to Y, per the two Switch games.
Despite knowing this, though, I still completely flubbed my first jump, embarrassingly landing in the water right in front of Mido (who is still an ass). On the whole though, I can't see what the removal of auto-jumping fundamentally changes to Ocarina other than potentially altering some puzzles, making returning players (me) remember to hit a button, and giving you another avenue for messing around. I spent five precious minutes of the preview attempting to jump atop Mido's house, for example. But that's what he deserves.
One change that might surprise returning players occurs in the dungeons. It's neither a full rework nor a 'Surprise! It's Master Quest all the way down.' In the Forest Temple, these changes manifest with Nintendo adding an elevator in the block puzzle room and removing the rotating pillars when you need to shoot an arrow through a torch to unfreeze a switch. Meanwhile, in the Great Deku Tree, there's now only one Skulltula barring your way to the woody depths and the vines leading to the Dungeon Map have been cut down (I never understood why those vines existed in the first place when there was a perfectly good ladder nearby…) I did notice more, but won't ruin future guides material.
As a dedicated Ocarina fan, spotting these changes was quite fun. None of them ever felt like they were robbing the game of something, either. Instead, they felt more like Nintendo has been filling in the cracks to make the ground more solid beneath my feet, especially since each of the dungeon's identities are still firmly intact. While I wasn't allowed to complete the quest, Inside The Deku Tree remains a great tutorial dungeon where you get to grips with combat and puzzle-solving. In this Switch 2 remake, it's also where returning players can get used to using the quick item select menu - another modernisation brought over from BOTW and TOTK here used for Link's full arsenal. It paired nicely with the Forest Temple, which I played in full, where the first dungeon's warnings about future dangers truly come home.
The Forest Temple has always been one of my favourite Ocarina dungeons. I love hunting down the Poe Sisters in their paintings, evading gruesome Floor Masters in the twisted rooms, and how the music sounds like someone is whispering just out of earshot. Close enough to hear, but too far to understand. It creates this deliciously eerie atmosphere - a worry that each step you take is the wrong one - and the new graphics elevate this sensation when you encounter the beautiful stained glass domed ceilings. The colours shine so brightly, creating a perfect contrast to the decaying house surrounding you. Stare for too long, wondering when Hyrule's National Trust is going to put any effort into building maintenance, and you might get nabbed by a disembodied hand. Thus is the danger of exploring a haunted, unexplained, manor. (Seriously, what is the Forest Temple? I have my theories but nearly every Ocarina dungeon has a small explanation bar this one. Did someone really build a house in a place called the Lost Woods thinking nothing would happen? Stellar behaviour. Love it.)
Then, of course, there's the temple's boss, Phantom Ganon. The paintings looming over you as Phantom Ganon begins his menacing approach before bursting from the canvas. A split second to send an arrow flying before he retreats back into the paint. It doesn't take long for the phantom to lose his patience, though, and energy ball tennis begins. Timing means everything, with failure resulting in a nasty shock. Eventually, Ganon falls to his knees to become victim to the vicious slashes of the Master Sword. What a fight, so gloriously recreated it was as if it was torn from my own memory. Sadly, I must admit a personal blunder. I was so caught up in the moment I forgot to check if you can still reflect his energy balls with an empty bottle. My apologies.
It's not just the dungeons which have seen alterations, Hyrule itself has been rebuilt for this iteration of Ocarina. Some changes barely affect the area - like Kokiri Forest's landbridge having a new starting point - while others literally change your perspective on a location.
Removing the fixed camera in Hyrule Castle Town has allowed the developers to enrich the settlement with life. Free from a forced bird's-eye view or being cemented to a fountain. You spot wanted posters in the backalleys, finally properly enjoy the view from the main square's balcony, and wonder how in Hylia's name the Happy Mask Salesman got permission for such an unsettling storefront. Ever wondered what was opposite the jar room? Turns out it's a stable! (Someone please tell me I'm not the only person who's thought about this.) Some of the characters have been moved as well; a few finding new homes, while others wonder about the streets. Hyrule Castle Town truly feels like a bustling capital, a place you'll visit for purposes outside of Rupee farming the jar room. But it's not where my favourite changes can be found.
I can still remember the first time I visited Hyrule Field. The sweeping fields and castle on the horizon promising adventure, me blissfully unaware of the owl. Now I know the field so well I could draw it from memory. Yet, when I visited it during the preview, Hyrule Field wasn't what I expected. All of the major locations - Lake Hylia, Kakariko Village etc. - were where they should be, but the geography between them had changed. Wheat now grows in the pastures surrounding Lon Lon Ranch and I found a dilapidated building near the Hyrule Castle Town moat. Even though the sun was shining, I wasn't safe either. Little Peahat Larva - flying plants with spikes - appeared from nowhere to attack Link. (And no, I wasn't always near a big Peahat when this occurred.) The six trees which once watched over the path leading from Kokiri Forest were also gone. I'm not sure how I feel about that. I've always loved those trees - they feel like the forest saying one last goodbye to Link. Though the stream in their place is quite pretty.
I didn't get to fully explore Hyrule Field. Partly due to time, partly because the Nintendo employees were very good at catching me whenever I ventured too close to an off-limits area. One new addition I did uncover, though, was an abandoned camp hidden away in the nock of a cliff. There I found a note left by a fairy, which Navi translated. It turned out to be a hint about rolling into trees. I wouldn't be surprised if there are more scattered about Hyrule. While the rest of the notes are most likely also hints, it would be nice if the developers have used them to provide more (read: any) characterisation for Navi.
I mentioned earlier I couldn't tell you how many hours I've spent playing Ocarina of Time. That's because I enjoyed a long phase where I would boot up the game and ignore the dungeons in favour of exploring. Sometimes I would revisit my favourite locations looking for secrets, others I would craft a new adventure for Link in my head and act it out. The world felt so brilliantly full, with new surprises around every corner. This feeling naturally faded over time as my brain logged every tidbit of information I found. Yet, I felt this burst of nostalgia and homecoming when I first entered Hyrule Field during the preview; standing on the border of a world I know so well, but, at the same time, barely know at all.
One aspect of the remake I wasn't fond of, however, was the English voice acting. It reminds me of a cheesy late '90s to early '00s anime dub, and not in a good way. And that's a shame given Ocarina's original 1998 release, you'd think this tone would be quite fitting. Luckily, behind every over the top English dub is a great sub. Yes, you can change the voice language.
The Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake is like returning to your hometown after a long absence. At first sight everything is as it should be and you believe you can navigate it, eyes shut. The longer you're there, though, the more unfamiliar it becomes. Was that shop here last time? Where does this sign lead? Is that grave new? Unbeknownst to you, the ground has shifted beneath your feet, transporting you to unknown territory. The question is - do you like the land you've found yourself in?
I love what I've played so far. Every change feels like it has a purpose; from the graphics painting Hyrule anew to the familiar music tinged with freshness. To the souls who discovered Zelda through BOTW and/or TOTK, I say give Ocarina a chance. This game is the foundation of the modern 3D adventure genre, and I doubt you'll regret visiting it. For myself, I'm looking forward to exploring this Ocarina's Hyrule and uncovering more of its secrets. Though I'm still not sure how I feel about those missing trees.
Nintendo offered both travel and accommodation for attending this preview event.

item.title: It looks like the owl known Kaepora Gaebora - part-tutorial, part-tip giver - will be far less talkative in the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read more
item.description:
It looks like the owl known Kaepora Gaebora - part-tutorial, part-tip giver - will be far less talkative in the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Who is the most dangerous monster you face in Ocarina of Time? 'Ganondorf' you'll surely answer. Wrong. 'Koume and Kotake', you might offer. After all, they raised Ganondorf and set him down his evil path. Incorrect. 'Okay, then it must be the Shadow Temple boss, the dastardly Bongo Bongo'. You fool. The most vicious villain can only be Kaepora Gaebora, the owl.
Sure, he appears helpful. Some might even say he's secretly Rauru, Sage of Light, but show me the evidence! (So I can ignore it). You might even use the lift he offers down Death Mountain to excuse his overly long explanations, but, never forget, always beware owls bearing free flights.
Seriously, think about it. What's the best, sneakiest, way to slow down the Hero of Time? A monster ambush? You can easily slay those beasts with a few sword slashes. But being captured in a one-sided conversation… one that forces you to slam the A button - because you already know how the map works and definitely know where you're going - only to suddenly be asked whether you want to hear all of that guff again… Of course you don't. Who would? But you've already hit A so you're going to hear it again and again and again. Slowly the edges of your soul begin to tatter and, with every loose thread, your desire to escape wanes until you simply give up. All that remains is one very smug owl.
I know I'm not the only person that's been trapped in an endless circle of 'Did you get all that?' at the behest of this cursed avian. But it seems our collective suffering is at an end. During my preview of the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake, I was very, very, worried about meeting the owl. I only had 15 minutes to explore both Hyrule Field and Hyrule Castle Town. A small amount of time which could easily get cut even shorter if I made one bad decision. I could feel Kaepora Gaebora circling above me as if I was a field mouse and he, well, an owl.
When the time came, I took a deep breath. I would pay attention. I would not fall for his 'yes means no, no means yes' trap. Not this time. Yet the damned owl surprised me: the conversation was short. Pleasant even. Not a single mention of the map was made and, before I knew it, the owl was flying away.
I can't say whether the owl's incessant talking has been cut down in other points in the game, but it would track with the other quality-of-life changes made to Ocarina of Time in this remake. (There's an Ocarina of Time preview waiting for you if you'd like to learn more. Nudge, nudge, wink, wink.) What we do know is that he's been fitted with a new design and, thanks to the game's trailer, will still offer flights from Lake Hylia.
For now, we'll just have to wait until the remake is released on 5th November to learn exactly how talkative the owl actually is.

item.title: Max Payne 3 is a bit of a strange project. Unlike its two predecessors, the game wasn't developed by original creator Remedy Entertainment, rather it was the product of Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption studio Rockstar Games. Read more
item.description:
Max Payne 3 is a bit of a strange project. Unlike its two predecessors, the game wasn't developed by original creator Remedy Entertainment, rather it was the product of Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption studio Rockstar Games.
Despite that pedigree, it is seen as something of a failure - or, at least, not quite what fans wanted from the third game in the iconic third-person shooter series. And Dan Houser, co-founder of Rockstar, says it was his fault.
In a wide-ranging interview with IGN, Houser, who was also Max Payne 3's lead writer, recalled his experience working on the game and how it differed from other Rockstar projects.
"It was a linear game, so it was a little different from writing an open-world game, a little more structured," Houser said. "I really enjoyed that as an experience. I loved what we did design-wise, the way the game didn't have loads, the way it felt like a 12-hour movie, some of the visual stuff we did with words on screen. I felt we were creating a really cool digital noir experience, and the consensus at the time was that people hated it."
Houser is being a little harsh here; Max Payne 3 was critically acclaimed at launch. The same stylistic, tonal and visual choices many didn't like are what also set it apart from the two prior games. Indeed, Max Payne 3's mechanics remain among the series' best to this day, with smooth third-person movement and sharp gunplay that make it a joy to play over 14 years later.
"I know Sam Lake [creator of Max Payne] well, and he's a very good guy and really talented. I thought we'd done a good job of doing another Max Payne game," Houser added. "Some people liked it; lots didn't. So we got it wrong, or I got it wrong. I failed. My bit was not a success."
Max Payne 3 is seen as a commercial disappointment by publisher Take-Two, who said its "lower than expected sales" were mainly responsible for a loss of $110m (~£82,9m) that financial quarter. Houser acknowledged the lower sales in the interview, saying "it wasn't as successful as it should have been".
"So I would say a large amount of that failure was on me as one of the people making the decisions and also as the writer, when people really missed [Sam Lake]'s writing," Houser added.
Years after Max Payne 3's release, Remedy and Rockstar would be reunited on a mega-project: a remake of Max Payne 1 and 2, which Remedy said two years ago had entered full production. It is understood the remake is Remedy's next project.

item.title: The ongoing employment tribunal between Grand Theft Auto 6 developer Rockstar Games and IWBG union members laid off from the studio has been extended into November.. Read more
item.description:
The ongoing employment tribunal between Grand Theft Auto 6 developer Rockstar Games and IWBG union members laid off from the studio has been extended into November..
The case was initially meant to end this Friday, but due to questioning of witnesses running long, the courts have pushed back the much-anticipated closing submission dates into November. This is when both Rockstar and IWGB legal representatives will present their closing arguments to the judge for a final verdict to be cast.
This extension was granted for a handful of reasons, perhaps most importantly because of a request from Rockstar's lawyers to have additional time to crossexamine some of the laid-off employees. Meanwhile, this week, IWGB continues to cross-examine Rockstar witnesses in what is proving to be an eye-opening and lengthy process.
As part of this extension, two additional dates have been added to the trial, on the 17th and 18th of November. Notably, this is one day prior to the release of GTA 6. Whether this is good or bad for Rockstar or the IWGB we'll have to wait and see. Maybe noise around the game's release will attract more attention to the case, or maybe it will drown it out.
The employment tribunal stems from the sudden firing of over 30 Rockstar employees in late 2025 for alleged gross misconduct, all of whom were present in a union Discord channel. The IWGB alleges this to be an effort to union-bust by Rockstar, whereas the developer claims it was due to the unauthorised sharing of information. Indeed, last Friday, one of the heads of Rockstar Lincoln claimed he was disinterested in evidence showing efforts to unionise in the run up to these firings, and was instead focused on other matters such as the formation of a union Twitter account.
How this case plays out is still up in the air. As one of the landmark legal cases in UK games industry history, the consequences of a Rockstar or IWGB win could reverberate for quite some time.

item.title: The video game layoffs continue. Ubisoft has announced it's closing Finnish studio RedLynx, creator of the Trials series of games, and that there's to be significant layoffs at Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced studio, Ubisoft Singapore. Read more
item.description:
The video game layoffs continue. Ubisoft has announced it's closing Finnish studio RedLynx, creator of the Trials series of games, and that there's to be significant layoffs at Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced studio, Ubisoft Singapore.
"Today, we informed our teams of a proposal to close RedLynx in Finland, subject to the local change negotiation process, which would affect up to 52 positions," Ubisoft said in a statement seen by Eurogamer. "At Ubisoft Singapore, 70 positions have been impacted to align the studio with upcoming production needs. The studio remains an important part of Ubisoft's global production organisation."
Ubisoft added: "We deeply value the contributions of both teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting our teams throughout this process and conducting it with care and respect."
Ubisoft didn't expand on its reasons for closing RedLynx, but the studio's last major standalone release was 2019's Trials Rising, suggesting it might have played more of a support role since then. Ubisoft has also been undergoing a top-to-bottom reorganisation of its business, shuffling a number of major franchises under new subsidiary company Vantage, while stretching the Ubisoft Massive label to cover more of its brands.
Ubisoft acquired RedLynx back in 2011, after the breakout success of Trials HD - a motorbike platform game with strong puzzle elements. Eurogamer loved Trials HD and I visited RedLynx shortly after its release to find out more about where the idea came from. The studio's leaders then, Tero Virtala and Antti Ilvessuo, have since moved on. Virtala notably became CEO of Remedy Entertainment (a post he recently left), and Ilvessuo - the creator of Trials - established new studio Channel 37 to make watery crafting survival game The Last Caretaker. That game appears to have done well in early access on Steam, by the way, and now approaches a spring 2027 1.0 release, on both PC and Xbox.
Ilvessuo, in response to today's news, said this to Eurogamer: "I'm proud of what we built at RedLynx, but my part in that story ended years ago. In 2012, Trials Evolution's riddle started, and its final chapter is set in 2113. So even something we made back then still has most of its future ahead of it.
"I don't know who - or what - will open that box. But someone has to care enough to carry the key all that way. That's what matters. Making something that will still mean something, something that has weight and history in a world that may be totally different in the future. Onwards!"
Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced, meanwhile, seemed popular, coasting past 3.5 million sales in only a fortnight, and a Switch 2 version is reportedly on the way. Dom scored the game three out of five stars in our Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced review.

item.title: Rockstar Games has revealed the original codename for Grand Theft Auto 6 was Project Americas, and that its intention was for the game to cover large areas of land in both the north of the country and the south. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games has revealed the original codename for Grand Theft Auto 6 was Project Americas, and that its intention was for the game to cover large areas of land in both the north of the country and the south.
The information comes from a wide-ranging interview with Rockstar on Bloomberg, which charted the beginnings of the GTA 6 project as well as the notable moments since: delays, game leaks, trailer releases, and more.
Bloomberg heard that Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson took a group of staff to Miami in 2015 for the game's first research trip, and that Project Americas - as the game was then known - "aimed to feature big swaths of land across both North and South America", before being scaled down to Miami and its surrounding areas. The original idea was to develop the game alongside Red Dead Redemption 2, but as the western project grew in scope and ambition, Project Americas was pushed back several years.
But lots changed after the release of Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar would nearly double in size, for starters - moving from 2,441 employees to 4,711 across 12 offices, the article noted. Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser, who'd written many of the previous GTA games, also left the company, prompting promotions for Nelson, Aaron Garbut, and Phil Hooker, who stepped into head of development roles.
By 2019, Rockstar had the skeleton of GTA 6 and the dual-protagonist hook of Jason and Lucia living their crime fantasy together, but the more granular details and mechanical intricacies of the game took longer, especially when the Covid-19 pandemic hit, forcing people to work from home. "Trying to keep a team together through that is really challenging," Nelson said.
Red Dead Redemption 2 also painted Rockstar as a company working with extreme levels of crunch - something Tom Phillips revealed in an investigation for Eurogamer. Rockstar acknowledged this in the Bloomberg interview, with Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar's head of publishing, stating it was "a real moment for Rockstar to look at itself".
"We all looked at each other and said, 'We're not doing it again like this,'" she added. "It's not been perfect, but it's certainly better than Red Dead 2 was. Anytime I say we haven't crunched, someone is going to say, 'I did.' And I don't want to get into arguments with individual teams or individual people. But I think we did things differently, and I'm proud of that."
Bloomberg reportedly spoke to "dozens" of Rockstar employees who "mostly expressed positive sentiment" regarding what Kolbe said, acknowledging improvements in areas such as crunch and removing managers who were abusive or tough to work with. However, Rockstar is currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland after unceremoniously firing 34 employees - 31 of them from its Rockstar North office - for what it alleged was gross misconduct but the fired employees called union-busting. We've been covering the tribunal's hearings as they've happened. It's now scheduled to conclude in November.
In relation to the ongoing attempts at unionisation, Kolbe offered a glimmer of hope, stating, "We go where the team goes,” she says. "So if they want a union, they will have a union."
As GTA 6 began to take shape, Rockstar suffered one of its biggest setbacks ever, as a phishing attack gained access to the company's Slack in 2022 and leaked unfinished footage of the game. Aaron Garbut said in response: "It feels like somebody's wading through your dirty washing. It's like they're inside your head. You see your early work out there. Nobody's ever supposed to see that. It's really weirdly invasive. And so it's quite hard to deal with on an emotional level."
As development progressed, it became clear Rockstar needed more time to finish the game. GTA 6's first trailer, aired in 2023, promised the game would be released in 2025, but Rockstar would move this date to May 2026 to allow more time. Then Rockstar realised it wouldn't be able to finish the game in time for that date either. Kolbe recalled phoning Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar's owner Take-Two, to tell him the news.
"I think he said, 'You're kidding. Please tell me you're kidding,'" Kolbe recalled. "But once we talked through why, he got it. And I think we are really lucky that he is as reasonable as he is, because a lot of people would say, 'You'd just better figure out how to ship it.' And we have been really, really lucky that we have not found ourselves in that place, because that happens to a lot of teams, and we've all played those games. It's not great."
GTA 6 is now finally due to release 19th November on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X, with a PC version reportedly due Q1 next year.

item.title: The original Destiny never made it to PC, but the shooter-MMO may not stay locked to PS4 and Xbox One for much longer. Some crafty modders have been working to get the game running on PC, and their efforts recently caught the eye of Bungie, which surprisingly didn't result in a take-down - not yet, at least. Read more
item.description:
The original Destiny never made it to PC, but the shooter-MMO may not stay locked to PS4 and Xbox One for much longer. Some crafty modders have been working to get the game running on PC, and their efforts recently caught the eye of Bungie, which surprisingly didn't result in a take-down - not yet, at least.
YouTuber Flummoxed has been sharing progress updates, and recently showed footage of various parts of Destiny 1 running on PC at 4K resolution at well over 60fps. The footage has a wider FOV than the one on console, meaning the build has been upgraded compared to consoles.
It is worth taking Deane's nod for what it is and not jump to conclusions. This is not confirmation of a Destiny 1 revival within Bungie, and I'd be surprised if Sony doesn't issue DMCA take-downs soon.
You may remember Deane from the recent Bungie apology video in which the studio's new leadership, Deane included, vowed to restore Destiny 2 content that's been removed over the years.
Considering how understaffed Bungie appears to be, and how it also has to split its attention between Destiny 2 and Marathon, a Destiny 1 release on PC is not likely to be on the studio's current list of priorities.
As for the project itself, it's dubbed Project Golden Age and it works backwards from client and server requests and responses to essentially rebuild the game. Fan projects have utilised similar techniques in the past to keep servers running for online-only games after their shutdowns, such as Anthem. Golden Age does, however, appear to use generative AI, with Claude's markdown tool mentioned on the project's GitLab page. The end result is not perfect yet, with a few physics and rendering issues, but it's the closest thing we have to Destiny 1 on PC.

item.title: World of Warcraft executive producer Holly Longdale has spoken at PAX Australia ahead of World of Warcraft: Forever's imminent release. Of note were her comments on the sheer popularity of the beta and how the team is handling the waves of feedback from early players. Read more
item.description:
First reported by PCGamesN, Longdale called the influx of players to the World of Warcraft: Forever beta "insane", and that there had been "no beta bigger than this" in Blizzard's history. This matches previous statements made by Longdale following a server cap increase made to the WoW Forever beta almost immediately after its release.
Longdale then moved onto the subject of feedback from this beta, and said that while Blizzard was"delighted" by the levels of engagement, the company had to be selective about what it listened to. "Social media when these MMOs came out wasn't really a thing, so we had some very focused areas where we got feedback. Now feedback comes from everywhere," she said. "And I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"
It's worth noting the Forever team has been quick in applying changes to the beta as feedback has come in. One recent example is the Skyborne elf models, which are being overhauled to fit better with the retro Classic WoW style. There have also been dungeon loot changes, drastically altered spell buffs (shout-out to the druids), and other tweaks over the past few weeks. This, per Longdale, stemmed from a combination of community-sourced info and data-driven research.
Even so, it appears WoW Forever is being made in the knowledge not everyone will be happy with decisions made. As Longdale put it: "You just have to accept that you're not going to make everybody happy. We have to make some calls, determine, 'What is our game? What is it for? Who is it for?' We have to try and walk that line as much as possible because otherwise you'll give a lot of people a little bit, instead of a complete experience."
World of Warcraft: Forever seems to have captured the hearts of both lapsed and consistent WoW players alike, even though it differs significantly from both modern WoW version and the Classic re-releases. Whether it can retain a strong community after it fully releases on the 4th November remains the big question.

item.title: Former game-seller Zavvi could be about to close for good; the company announced it has entered administration and that it has ceased trading while the insolvency process is resolved. Read more
item.description:
Former game-seller Zavvi could be about to close for good; the company announced it has entered administration and that it has ceased trading while the insolvency process is resolved.
Zavvi announced the news in a boilerplate message on its website, announcing BDO LLP as the company handling the administration process. The message reiterated that: "[Zavvi] is unable to fulfil any outstanding orders or pre-orders. Please also note that we are unable to accept any returns for items of any kind.
"We appreciate that customers who have paid for goods that have not been received will be concerned about their orders and payments," the message added, before suggesting that those customers contact their bank, card issuer or payment providers "to establish whether they may be entitled to recover their payment". A customer inquiry email address has been set up but it sounds as though it'll mostly send an automated response.
Zavvi's intention to appoint administrators had been reported a month ago, with the alleged aim of "protecting the business and its stakeholders and securing the best possible outcome". Exactly what that means and whether it's a genuine play to save the company or ensure investors recoup money before it closes, remains to be seen. But this appointment of administrators - foreboding though it is - doesn't necessarily mean the end for Zavvi.
Zavvi was once a familiar name in video gaming. Zavvi formed when Virgin Megastores split from the Virgin company as an independent company in 2007, making it - at the time - one of the largest independent entertainment sellers in the UK. But the good times didn't last as barely a year later, Zavvi entered administration (for the first time). The Hut Group bought Zavvi out of administration in 2009, and the company pivoted more towards pop culture and entertainment sales thereafter.

item.description:
If the Planet Zoo series has taught me anything it's that I'm rubbish at animals. Sure, I'm okay with the simple stuff - I do, you'll be relieved to hear, know the difference between an elephant and a flamingo - but the more exotic they get, the second we start dabbling in subspecies, the more clueless I am. That was one of the joys of the original Planet Zoo: a chance to discover a vibrant menagerie of unusual animals, all brought to wonderful life by developer Frontier's typically exquisite artistry. And after spending some early hours with Planet Zoo 2, it's this, as much as anything, that's kept me so completely enthralled.
Did you know, for instance, there's such a thing as a tree kangaroo? Until about 24 hours ago, I did not! But here comes the little fella (or a convincingly lifelike digital recreation of one, at least), bounding enthusiastically across his enclosure, tail whipping adorably as he twirls up his wooden climbing frame, hugging the beams as he goes. I've lost many a delighted minute watching ring-tailed lemurs scamper, or Asian small-clawed otters launching themselves off rocks into pools. I've seen Masai giraffes unfold themselves in a complicated dance as they ready to explore the African savanna, and Hawksbill turtles drifting serenely around my aquarium as manatees inquisitively probe the depths. And the birds! Aviaries are now a thing, meaning I've gawped as practically prehistoric Majestic shoebills show off their extraordinary wingspans. And, yes, it's made me curious enough to Google these fascinating creatures' real-world counterparts in turn, so hello education.
There is, of course, more to Planet Zoo 2 than just looking, but it's hard not to get distracted by such exotic sights, especially when it's all rendered so beautifully. Whatever you might say about Frontier's sims when you start digging deeper into the gameplay stuff, it's impossible to knock the studio's presentational skills. And Planet Zoo 2 gets to be even showier this time. That starts with the new nature reserves; vast stretches of land where animals can roam free. In Africa, hippos bake happily in muddy waters; zebras graze under the cool shade of trees; elephants roam in busy herds, while flamingoes preen in shallow pools. And there I am - in a feature borrowed from Frontier's so-so Jurassic World Evolution series - thundering across the savanna with giddy abandon as I take in the sights, my little jeep careening down slopes and splashing through the water. 'Stop!' I'm suddenly commanded early on in the tutorial, 'take some photos!' And honestly, when it all looks this lovely, why wouldn't you?
Photographs, when snapped on expeditions like these, earn research points. It's another feature borrowed from Frontier's dinosaur series, and to be honest, it feels just as arbitrary here. And while I've really only played for a fistful of hours at this point (certainly not enough to have formed a conclusive opinion), the sense I'm getting is that Planet Zoo 2's big new bullet-point features - much like Planet Coaster 2's underbaked delve into water parks - aren't exactly game-changing, although the new animal types are certainly welcome. Aquariums are essentially just wetter enclosures that need an attached filtration pump to keep them clean and appropriately salinated (freshwater fish aren't going to be too happy if your H2O's salty, and you'll need to keep an eye on temperature and depth too). Aviaries aren't much more involved; they're covered enclosures requiring roof supports so there's enough space for your birds to stretch their wings. As for your nature reserves, ecosystems are pre-defined areas on a larger map that behave like shared habitats with a few more steps - basically enclosures, just barrier-free.
I'm being a touch reductive here, admittedly, but none of this is really a criticism. Unlike the Planet Coaster series, which has always placed park customisation first and foremost, with management depth a very distant second, Planet Zoo 1 was already a far richer, more robust sort of tycoon game, and that carries through to its sequel. Animal welfare is, again, a substantial undertaking in itself as you navigate everything from enclosure management (creating appropriate biomes, ensuring sufficient enrichment, and so on) to breeding, health, and even trading. But then there's a whole other side, as the animal stuff dovetails elegantly into the more familiar logistics of park management.
As ever, you'll need to hire the right staff to keep your zoo clean and well-maintained, and you'll work to keep guests satisfied: fulfilling their food, drink, energy, bladder, and education needs so they leave happy enough that the next lot of visitors aren't going to baulk at your entry fee. Economy is actually important here! And given that happy animals means happy guests, the Ouroboros loop is complete. It's a substantial enough, satisfying enough balancing act that I'm not really concerned the new stuff - the aviaries, aquariums, and reserves - feels more like textural finesse than radical change. And to be honest, I was sold on aquariums the second I saw you could build an underwater tunnel, Jaws 3 style.
There's a lot of other stuff I really like too. The tutorial campaign, for one, is excellent; I remember getting lost quite quickly in the original Planet Zoo as it haphazardly tackled the very basics before leaving me to muddle through. Here, Frontier's charmingly voiced cast of recurring characters patiently and thoroughly introduce you to all the important bits in clear, logical fashion as you bound across biomes and continents. And the UI, although still a little fussy, feels more intuitive, more navigable too, especially if you're using a controller.
There are welcome new features like the nature brush - particularly handy for larger enclosures, when you don't have the stamina to place 300 trees one-by-one. And seasons are a lovely addition, powdering your park with snow or giving it a more autumnal hue - even if I'm not sure how meaningfully the weather affects the management side of things right now. Frontier also seems to have learned its lesson from Planet Coaster 2, which launched in such an anaemic state (now much improved after fan outcry) it felt like a cynical ploy to flog post-launch DLC. Here though, builders and aesthetes get a more generous nine themes to tinker with at launch, and 136 different species of animals - some from Planet Zoo 1, some from its DLC, and some new.
And really, it all comes back to those animals. Planet Zoo 2 - with its gently paced blend of creative tinkering, strategic experimentation, and stimulating problem-solving - is already a wonderfully chilled endeavour; the perfect tonic, frankly, after several weeks of Scottish trauma horror, extra-dimensional BDSM fiends, and French Revolutionary War bloodshed. But then something catches my eye. Perhaps it's an African Savannah elephant noodling at the water's edge, or a Toco toucan, cheerfully hopping away to adventures new. Maybe it's a Blacktip reefshark, or a Sumatran orangutan, or a North Sulawesi babirusa. Regardless, I'm compelled to stop and watch their delightfully realised antics unfold. And, hey, I suddenly think to myself, I finally got its name right. Education through adorable osmosis, and all that. Animals are cool!

item.title: Xbox is reacting - uncharacteristically quickly - to the deluge of vibe-coded game ports, decompiles and recompiles we've been seeing online in recent weeks by establishing Xbox Labs, a new initiative seemingly designed to explore the phenomenon. Read more
item.description:
Xbox is reacting - uncharacteristically quickly - to the deluge of vibe-coded game ports, decompiles and recompiles we've been seeing online in recent weeks by establishing Xbox Labs, a new initiative seemingly designed to explore the phenomenon.
Xbox Labs was announced by CEO Asha Sharma in a message sent to staff and published on Xbox Wire. The initiative is led by Xbox chief technical officer (CTO) Scott Van Vliet, who previously led Azure for OpenAI at Microsoft.
So what is Xbox Labs? The announcement doesn't give a clear answer, with Sharma seemingly going out of her way to avoid mentioning AI or generative AI in the language.
"In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support," wrote Sharma. "Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another."
These "experiments" challenge long-held industry assumptions such as "the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games", Sharma added. And Xbox Labs was formed to "explore" that and more.
For now, Labs represents "a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists" who will "turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience", Sharma said."We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating."
Sharma added: "I think Xbox has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing Xbox games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide."
Xbox recently announced XP, a new division responsible for non-gaming partnerships like movie licensing and merchandising, consisting of four areas: Xbox Places, Xbox Pictures, Xbox Partnerships and Xbox Products.
The news also comes days after Google and Unity both announced gen-AI game-making platforms where users can supposedly create games using simple text prompts. Given how vague the Labs announcement is, it's not clear if Microsoft is interested in the same idea.

item.title: CD Projekt Red has released an update for The Witcher 3 Remastered on PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro, making "various stability improvements to help ensure a more reliable experience" to the game. And those are the entire patch notes for hotfix 5.01b, Eurogamer understands. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has released an update for The Witcher 3 Remastered on PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro, making "various stability improvements to help ensure a more reliable experience" to the game. And those are the entire patch notes for hotfix 5.01b, Eurogamer understands.
The update has drawn some concern from players waiting for the promised Switch 2 Witcher 3 update, prompting the studio to reassure people on X that: "We're working on getting the Nintendo Switch 2 patch to all users as soon as possible." That Switch 2 patch is said to improve visual "clarity and sharpness" in the game.
CD Projekt Red has been busy addressing issues with the Remastered edition of The Witcher 3 since it was released two weeks ago. It's a transformative update, significantly altering the game's visuals while also changing animations, skills, and even some gameplay. Given its breadth - and that it's free and occurring 11 years after the game's release - I called The Witcher 3 Remastered an extraordinarily generous upgrade after playing it, though the game's audience isn't entirely happy. Some feel it made the game too bright, though this aspect has been addressed in patches since release.
Incidentally, Digital Foundry has now chimed into the performance discussion with a full appraisal of The Witcher 3 Remastered on PC, complete with optimised settings suggestions. DF is also tracking the various changes being made to path tracing in the game, which so far is enormously system-heavy.
The Witcher 3 Remastered raises the game's visual standards ahead of the new Songs of the Past expansion arriving next year. This will bring a beautiful new region to explore, dozens of hours of gameplay, and a story revolving around Geralt's musical pal Dandelion and family. Dom had a chance to see Songs of the Past at Gamescom and came away impressed.

item.title: As American comedy series Saturday Night Live airs a sketch lampooning the November showdown between Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, a pair of former Nintendo employees have recalled a more infamous SNL sketch from years earlier that did not go down well at all. Read more
item.description:
As American comedy series Saturday Night Live airs a sketch lampooning the November showdown between Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, a pair of former Nintendo employees have recalled a more infamous SNL sketch from years earlier that did not go down well at all.
The older SNL sketch had controversial billionaire businessman Elon Musk dress as Nintendo character Wario, on trial for being evil, ironically enough. During the trial there were mentions of Mario taking drugs, blurred out Luigi dick pics, all while Wario-Musk tried to convince the courtroom he was misunderstood.
"That did not go over well," Krysta Yang said on the Kit and Krysta podcast (via Techradar). Yang was a former host of Nintendo Minute with Kit Ellis - the eponymous Kit in the podcast's title - and both worked within Nintendo for more than 10 years.
"We were still there for that," Ellis added. "That was one that was not beloved by the people ... That was not received well at Nintendo," Yang echoed..
Ellis said the Wario sketch came out of "leftfield" because it wasn't obviously tethered to anything, as there wasn't a Mario or Wario game releasing at that time. "Why is Elon Musk Wario?" Ellis recalled people wondering. "Some of the stuff was getting into subject matter that was uncomfortable for Nintendo."
Nintendo had nothing to do with the sketch, the pair insisted, "But there is a lot of contact between Nintendo and the producers of SNL, [and] these other late night shows. There are people who are very focused on that segment in particular within the communications team at Nintendo, making sure that they get games when they come out, that they have access to information."
In the most recent Zelda vs. GTA 6 sketch, Link and Jason - main characters in their respective games - argue about whose game is best. Yang and Ellis praised Link's costume - "This seemed to be custom-made to the remake," Ellis said - but the pair were more muted on the skit itself. "I thought this was generally fine," Yang said. "I wasn't rolling on the floor laughing or anything like that. There were some moments where it's a little cringey."
The Ocarina of Time remake was shown in some detail in September, ahead of its 5th November release. The game's art style has been updated considerably, which has been a topic of much debate, but there are changes to performance and to the ways the game works, as well. It's a notable undertaking.
Meanwhile, GTA 6 looms large for its 19th November release.

item.title: Sifu, Sloclap's 2022 martial arts action game, can now be played on smartphones. The French developer released the game today on Android and iOS, following an announcement earlier in the month. Read more
item.description:
Sifu, Sloclap's 2022 martial arts action game, can now be played on smartphones. The French developer released the game today on Android and iOS, following an announcement earlier in the month.
This portable version of Sifu is priced $8 / £6, and the studio said it has been developed specifically for phone screens. The game has new touch-based controls, as you might imagine, which translate its core moves to on-screen prompts, with environmental interactions streamlined.
The ports also have a new, adaptive camera which Sloclap said works better on smaller screens. The developer said it worked to retain Sifu's painterly look, and its fluid and impactful combat for the mobile release, but the game also supports controllers if you prefer.
Judging by the trailer, it does look like the Sifu we know, albeit with a softer image as a result of the less powerful hardware.
Sifu was critically acclaimed and sold 1 million copies in its first three weeks of release. Previously a PlayStation and Epic Games Store exclusive, Sifu made its way to Steam and Xbox a year later.
Sloclap followed Sifu with something altogether different: a third-person football game called Rematch. The game is likewise critically acclaimed and commercially successful, but its reveal left fans who were eager for a sequel to Sifu disappointed.
While Sloclap continues to support Rematch, the studio's future plans remain unknown. Sloclap's three developed games are all notably distinct. The studio's debut title, Absolver, is a martial arts MMO. Then came Sifu, a single-player kung fu game, which was followed up by a third-person football game in Rematch. It's anyone's guess what genre the studio is going to tackle next.

item.title: A new report suggests that GTA 6 will release on PC in "Q1 2027". That, at least, is what GamesBeat is saying, citing "sources familiar with the matter." Read more
item.description:
A new report suggests that GTA 6 will release on PC in "Q1 2027". That, at least, is what GamesBeat is saying, citing "sources familiar with the matter."
That means GTA 6 would enjoy anywhere between two-to-five months' worth of console exclusivity: it's launching on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19th November. We had a tease of the official PC version of the game from Strauss Zelnick earlier this year; the Take-Two boss noted that whilst the company tends not to "go across all platforms simultaneously", he was aware of the hunger for the game on non-console platforms.
This gap marks quite a small margin between one release and the other, however: GTA 5 released in September 2013 while the PC version (after initially aiming for simultaneous release) was delayed until April 2015. Red Dead Redemption 2 launched on 26th October, 2018 for consoles, but then came to PC over a year later (5th November, 2019). Rockstar has not, of course, confirmed this PC release date is real, so take all this with a pinch of salt for now.
There is potential that we could see a PC version of the game sooner: (in)famous leaker, CyberLeek, threatened to release a full, playable build of the game over the weekend. Whilst this could end up being an empty threat, it's clear the leaker has a genuine build of the game - the prolific leaks have even prompted Rockstar to issue a formal statement, and the company has reportedly tried to subpoena Discord as it tries to identify the person behind the leaks.
Whether this release date turns out to be true or not, it would make sense for Rockstar to get the PC version of the game in PC players' hands sooner rather than later - a large portion of the profit GTA 5 has hoovered up comes from GTA Online, and Rockstar is going to want to have a solid sales foundation for when it decides to deploy GTA 6 Online. Per Twitch CEO Dan Clancy, it seems the new version of GTA Online is lined up for a 2027 release date: "We spent a lot of time talking with Rockstar about their plans, and also helping them think about how they can engage our creators. You are going to see this big bump with GTA 6, but then an even bigger one next year when they launch multiplayer," he said in an interview earlier this year.
Amid the build-up to GTA 6's release, Rockstar Games and the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) are currently engaged in the final tribunal hearing relating to the sudden firing of 31 Rockstar North employees a year ago, allegedly as part of a union-busting initiative by Rockstar.

item.title: Dan Houser, one of Rockstar's co-founders that left the GTA 6 studio in 2020, has given a wide-ranging new interview with IGN, covering topics including the tortured production of Bully, changes made to Grand Theft Auto 3's artwork post-9/11, the reaction to Red Dead Redemption's ending, and why he thinks Max Payne 3 was a failure. Read more
item.description:
Dan Houser, one of Rockstar's co-founders that left the GTA 6 studio in 2020, has given a wide-ranging new interview with IGN, covering topics including the tortured production of Bully, changes made to Grand Theft Auto 3's artwork post-9/11, the reaction to Red Dead Redemption's ending, and why he thinks Max Payne 3 was a failure.
The most interesting to me is how the iconic boxart for GTA 3 - a template that has been used for every game since, by the way, most recently being co-opted for GTA 6's cover - was actually put together very last minute.
"What's funny is the cover art that became the iconic GTA cover art; Stephen Bliss did that in about two evenings because the old cover art was probably being too offensive to release after 9/11 because there were burning buildings in it," Houser revealed to IGN. "So it would've been fine if there hadn't just been 9/11. So that look of the shards, the squares that became very iconic, only appeared because of 9/11."
GTA 3 takes place in Liberty City - a thinly-veiled parody of the real-world New York City, where the 9/11 disaster, of course, took place. So there was sensitivity around showing destruction and death publicly in the months and years after. This is something that Rockstar had to consider carefully as it was launching the game into the aftermath of the event.
"There were a couple of bits of content that would've been fine, but in the exact aftermath of 9/11, were maybe a little bit too much," Houser explained. "So we had to take those out, and the team [rallied] round and remove those and edit a couple of lines of dialogue and did a quick content stand and thought it was fine. And then the game came out in October of 2001. It was gradual all the way through till Christmas 2001 into early 2002, and it just didn't stop selling. It's not like any single week was that massive. It was that every week it just rumbled on."
The art he's referring to (above) is, of course, as iconic as the staples of GTA 3's newly-open world gameplay. Houser notes this, and reflects: "GTA has become part of the wider cultural fabric. I mean, you sort of saw that on YouTube clips and whatever else that would have the HUD on it, and people using the logo and things like that. When you go to any big tourist resort, you'll have a sort of GTA cover art-inspired T-shirt available. So you began to see that creep in 10 years ago."
This isn't the first we've heard from Dan Houser in the past few months. Back in July, the Rockstar Games co-founder joined longtime GTA writer Lazlow Jones to espouse some opinions on the on-going physical games debate. "I don't know that I care," he responded when asked about the fact that Sony plans to scrap physical discs from January 20-28 onwards, "but if people want that, companies should provide it. I think the ability to update games - as critical as people are on digital releases - the ability to update and fix problems in games have been very useful to the quality of games."
Elsewhere, with his company Absurd Ventures, Houser is working on an "open world action-adventure". This is the first time we get a look at "just a few characters" coming to a "story-driven action-comedy adventure game set in the Absurdaverse".

item.title: Sony today announced a new version of its disc-less PlayStation 5 console. The console is getting a Midnight Black variant but it's sadly only been announced for the Japanese market. Read more
item.description:
Sony today announced a new version of its disc-less PlayStation 5 console. The console is getting a Midnight Black variant but it's sadly only been announced for the Japanese market.
As revealed on the Japanese PlayStation Blog, the Midnight Black PS5 Digital Edition launches on 19th November (yep, that's GTA 6's release date) for ¥55,000 (~$380 / £263).
If that price sounds cheap, it's because the new console is based on the region-locked PS5 Sony launched in Japan last November. The Digital Edition console's language cannot be changed from Japanese, and it only works with PSN accounts based in Japan, preventing it from being exported outside the country - hence the cheaper price.
Sony is also releasing a Midnight Black blu-ray disc drive to go along with the new console, for players who want to retain access to their physical media - for however long that's going to be worth it. Maybe the introduction of this new model will relieve the pressure Sony is facing with its PS5 Pro - a console so in-demand in Japan that the company has had to implement a lottery system in order to adequately effectively distribute supplies.
While the rest of the world does not have a Midnight Black PS5, you can replicate the look by buying the Midnight Black Console Covers, which cost $54 / £45. The PS5's covers can be easily removed and replaced. Seeing as the middle of the PS5 is already black, purchasing and installing these covers achieves the same effect, if you're so inclined. If you want to complete the collection, a Midnight Black DualSense controller is available for sale worldwide.
The only missing piece is the blu-ray disc drive, which is only available in the standard white colour. It's possible Sony is going to bring the Midnight Black version to the rest of the world after it launches in Japan.

item.title: Kazuo "Kaz" Hirai, who was the president of PlayStation from 2007 to 2012, apparently didn't pay much attention to orders he received from Sony's top brass. Read more
item.description:
Kazuo "Kaz" Hirai, who was the president of PlayStation from 2007 to 2012, apparently didn't pay much attention to orders he received from Sony's top brass.
Hirai recently revealed this in a conversation published in Japanese publication Nikkei XTrend, as translated by Game Observer. "When I was president of Sony Computer Entertainment handling the PlayStation home console business, whenever Howard [Stringer] and the other executives told me this or that, I went my own way, saying, 'What the headquarters says is irrelevant. We are PlayStation,'" Hirai revealed, reportedly while laughing.
Hirai would later succeed Stringer in leading the entirety of Sony, though, which he recalled was a time of struggle for the company that necessitated a change in direction.
"The first things I focused on were: 'getting people to know me' and 'getting them to move in the same direction," Hirai revealed. "Without respect, no one is going to think, 'Let's work hard together!'"
Ironically, as Sony CEO, Hirai wanted to prevent the different divisions from doing what he used to do at PlayStation. The executive wanted everyone to work towards a unified goal, rather than each doing their own thing. He famously came up with the 'kando' slogan, based on the Japanese word that means being emotionally moved by something. It was a corporate strategy to encourage staff to create products and experiences that touch people's feelings and not just function well.
Hirai's tenure as PlayStation president saw him lead the gaming division during a key period in its history. He took over shortly after the launch of the PlayStation 3, the rocky launch of the PlayStation Vita, and the infamous PlayStation outage in 2011. Hirai stepped down as Sony CEO in 2018. He is also known for the much lampooned and memed PlayStation E3 2006 press conference.

item.description:
UPDATE 4.20PM BST: Eurogamer understands that this meeting took place and the transcription is correct, with the exception of the word "revive". The transcript should read: "We will not survive if we only rely on the past."
ORIGINAL STORY 11.30AM BST: Xbox leader Asha Sharma has reportedly broadcast her intent to "create enduring new IP" alongside the company's much publicised plan to organise around its biggest gaming brands - think The Elder Scrolls, think Blizzard, etc. But according to Sharma: "We will not survive if we only revive on the past."
Sharma reportedly said this in addition to dropping more information about Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix and while reflecting on Xbox's "return to growth" after "an all-time low".
"We're backing our strongest franchises," Sharma allegedly said. "I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences."
It's a declaration which seems at odds with Xbox's recent actions. Parting ways with studios like Double Fine and Compulsion, and probably Arkane - all of which have a track record in creating new game ideas such as Keeper and South of Midnight, and Dishonored and Deathloop - seems an odd way to go about engendering a culture of courage in creation. Similarly, having an inventive studio like Obsidian work under Bethesda making a Fallout game suggests there's no immediate room there to pursue wholly original ideas. But at least Xbox is investing in Hideo Kojima's Physint, right? Right?
Cuts at id Software and consolidation elsewhere across the Xbox gaming division also reflect a company that appears to be reorganising around its biggest gaming brands rather than one intent on taking new, creative risks. Indeed, a look at Xbox's upcoming roster really only reveals InXile's Clockwork Revolution - one of its two Xbox exclusives - as an obvious contender in the 'big new idea' area. But will it be strong enough to start a lasting series?
Meanwhile, the studio behind the other Xbox exclusive, Gears of War: E-Day, fears for its future after releasing its game, despite it seeming to have been a success. That's because of the hundreds of impending cuts Microsoft still intends to make to its Xbox division. There, uncertainty looms large.
Dom reviewed Gears of War: E-Day for us recently and, generally, really enjoyed it. "Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too," Dom wrote.
